tagline: A tale of exile, court intrigue, and reversal in which a Jewish queen and her cousin save their people from annihilation in the Persian Empire, and God is never named.
overview:
Esther is set in the Persian royal city of Susa during the reign of Xerxes, the king the Hebrew text calls Ahasuerus. It tells how a young Jewish orphan named Hadassah, known by her Persian name Esther, becomes queen after the king deposes his first wife, Vashti; how her cousin and guardian Mordecai refuses to bow to the king's new favorite, Haman; how Haman, in revenge, obtains a royal decree to wipe out every Jew in the empire on a single day chosen by lot; and how Esther, at the risk of her life, goes to the king unsummoned and turns the plot back on the man who made it. Haman dies on the gallows he built for Mordecai, the Jews are given the right to defend themselves, and the day marked for their destruction becomes a day of rescue.

The book ends by explaining the Jewish festival of Purim, named for the pur, the lot Haman cast. Purim is still kept every year, and at it the whole scroll of Esther is read aloud. In Jewish tradition Esther is one of the five Megillot, the festival scrolls, and it is often simply called the Megillah, the scroll.

The most striking thing about Esther is what it leaves out. In the Hebrew text God is never mentioned. No one prays by name, no prophet speaks, no miracle happens, and the covenant, the law, the temple, and Jerusalem are barely in view. Yet the story is full of timing too exact to be chance: a sleepless night, a record read at the right page, a queen in the right place. The book asks its readers, many of whom also lived as a minority under foreign power, to see the hand of a God who is hidden but not absent.
author: The book does not name its author. The Babylonian Talmud assigns its writing to the men of the Great Assembly, the body of leaders that Jewish tradition places in the Persian period after the return from exile. Some older Christian and Jewish writers suggested Mordecai himself, since Esther 9:20 says he recorded these events, but that verse refers to his letters establishing Purim rather than to the book. Modern scholars generally regard the author as an unknown Jewish writer, most likely living in the eastern Diaspora (the scattered Jewish communities outside the land of Israel), who knew Persian court life, vocabulary, and administration well.
date: The story is set in the reign of Xerxes I, who ruled Persia from about 486 to 465 BC. The book itself must have been written after his reign, since it looks back on his days (1:1). Many scholars date its composition to the late Persian period, around the fourth century BC, because its Hebrew belongs to the later stages of the language, it uses a number of Persian loanwords, and it shows no sign of the Greek culture that spread through the region after Alexander the Great's conquests in the 330s BC. Others place it in the early Hellenistic period, in the third or second century BC. A Greek version with substantial additions was circulating by the first century BC.
setting:
The Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, stretched from India in the east to Egypt, Cush (the upper Nile region), and western Asia Minor in the west. Cyrus had allowed exiled Jews to return to Judah in 539/538 BC, but many stayed where they had settled in Babylonia and Persia. Esther concerns those who stayed. Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of the empire's royal capitals, and French excavations there uncovered the great palace complex begun by Darius I and used by Xerxes.

Xerxes is well known from the Greek historian Herodotus, who describes his invasion of Greece in 480 BC and its failure at Salamis and Plataea. The feast of Esther 1 falls in Xerxes' third year, before that campaign, and Esther comes to the king in his seventh year, after it. The book's picture of the court fits what is known of Persian government: satraps and governors over provinces, a royal courier system, edicts sent in every local script and language, a king kept at a distance by eunuchs and protocol, and advisers who ranked by their access to him. In chronological terms the events fall between Ezra 6 (the temple's completion in 515 BC) and Ezra 7 (Ezra's return, traditionally dated to about 458 BC).
purpose: The book's stated purpose is to explain and establish Purim, so that the memory of the deliverance would not fade from Jewish descendants (9:28). Beneath that, it served Jews living scattered through a foreign empire. It showed that a Jew could serve faithfully at a pagan court without ceasing to belong to God's people, that hatred of the Jews could arise suddenly and be written into law, and that their survival did not depend on having a king, a temple, or even visible signs of God's presence. For readers who had no prophet and saw no miracles, it taught them to look for God's care in the ordinary turns of history.
story: Esther belongs to the period after the exile, alongside Ezra and Nehemiah. Those books follow the Jews who went back to rebuild Jerusalem; Esther follows those who remained in the east. Its conflict reaches back to much older chapters of Israel's story. Mordecai is introduced as a Benjaminite descended from a man named Kish, a name that recalls the family of King Saul, and Haman is an Agagite, which recalls Agag the Amalekite king whom Saul spared against God's command in 1 Samuel 15. The Amalekites had attacked Israel on the road out of Egypt (Exodus 17), and God had promised war against them from generation to generation. Esther's story replays that old enmity, and this time the descendant of Kish does not fail. The book also stands behind the whole later history of the Jewish people: had Haman's plan succeeded, there would have been no people from whom the promised Messiah could come.
christ: Esther contains no direct prophecy of the Messiah, and it is best to say plainly that its links to Christ are patterns rather than predictions. The largest pattern is the preservation of the people through whom God had promised to bless all nations (Genesis 12:3). The book is one chapter in a long story of threats to Abraham's line and God's quiet keeping of it, a story the New Testament sees completed when Jesus is born a Jew under another empire. Christians have also noticed the shape of Esther's act: one person, placed at the center of power, risks death by going in to the king on behalf of a people condemned by a law they cannot undo, and they are saved. Esther is not a picture of Christ in any detailed sense, and she can only plead, while Christ gives himself. But the story's great reversal, in which the day set for death becomes a day of joy, is the shape the Gospels give to the cross and the empty tomb.
reading:
Esther is a carefully crafted narrative, and much of its meaning comes through its craft. Watch for banquets (the book is full of them, and the plot turns at them), for the irony of characters who get the opposite of what they intend, and for reversals, which the book itself names in 9:1 when the enemies' plan is overturned. The silence about God is deliberate, and a reader should notice where the story seems to hold its breath for him: Mordecai's word that relief may come from another place (4:14), Esther's three-day fast (4:16), the king's sleepless night (6:1).

The book has been read in different ways. Many readers take it as a historical account from the Persian court; others see it as a historical novella built around real institutions and possibly real events, written to explain a festival. Both groups agree that its purpose is theological as well as historical. Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. One is to treat Esther and Mordecai as flawless models; the text presents them with concealment, compromise, and ambition as well as courage. The other is to read the fighting in chapter 9 as a license for revenge; the book stresses that the Jews acted under a royal edict to defend themselves and did not touch the plunder. Readers of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles will also find six longer Greek additions, including prayers of Mordecai and Esther that name God; Protestant and Jewish Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew text.

structure.title: A new queen in Susa
structure.summary: Xerxes deposes Vashti after she refuses his summons, and Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by Mordecai, is chosen as queen without revealing her people. Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king, and his deed is recorded.

structure.title: Haman's decree and Mordecai's challenge
structure.summary: Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, who obtains a decree to destroy all the Jews on a day chosen by lot. Mordecai urges Esther to go to the king, and she resolves to go, fasting and at the risk of her life.

structure.title: Banquets and the great reversal
structure.summary: Esther invites the king and Haman to two banquets. On the night between them the king cannot sleep, Mordecai is honored by Haman himself, and at the second banquet Esther exposes Haman, who is hanged on his own gallows.

structure.title: A counter-decree and the feast of Purim
structure.summary: Mordecai is given Haman's authority and issues a decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves. On the appointed day they prevail over their enemies, and Mordecai and Esther establish Purim as a yearly festival.

structure.title: The greatness of Mordecai
structure.summary: A brief epilogue records Mordecai's high rank under Xerxes and his work for the good of his people.

themes.title: Hidden providence
themes.body: God is not named, yet the story is built from coincidences that no one arranges: Esther's rise before the danger appears, Mordecai overhearing a plot, a king who cannot sleep on the one night it matters, a record opened to the right place. The book invites readers to see these as the work of a God who governs history without always showing himself. For people living far from the temple and without prophets, this was a way of believing that God had not stopped caring for them.

themes.title: Reversal
themes.body: The book's plot is a series of turnings upside down. Haman plans honor for himself and has to give it to Mordecai; he builds a gallows for Mordecai and dies on it; a decree of destruction is answered by a decree of defense; mourning becomes feasting. The narrator names the pattern when he says the enemies' plan was overturned (9:1). The reversals teach that the powers who seem to control history do not have the last word.

themes.title: Identity under pressure
themes.body: Esther begins by hiding who she is and ends by naming her people before the king at the risk of her life. Mordecai, by contrast, will not bow to Haman and openly says he is a Jew. The book explores what it costs to belong to God's people in a culture that rewards blending in, and it treats the moment when concealment has to end as the moment of true courage.

themes.title: Law, power, and the vulnerable
themes.body: Persian law in Esther cannot be revoked, and it is used by powerful men to settle personal grievances: a queen deposed for refusing to be displayed, an entire people condemned because one man would not bow. The book shows how easily law can be turned into an instrument of pride and hatred, and how those with some access to power are responsible for those who have none.

themes.title: Remembering deliverance
themes.body: The book closes by turning a rescue into a festival, with feasting, gifts to one another, and gifts to the poor. Remembering is itself an act of faith: each Purim retells the story so that later generations, facing their own Hamans, would know they had been preserved before.

keyChapters.why: Esther becomes queen while hiding her identity, and Mordecai's unrewarded rescue of the king is recorded, setting up everything that follows.
Haman's decree to destroy the Jews reveals the depth of the threat and ties the story to the ancient conflict between Israel and Amalek.
Mordecai's challenge that Esther may have come to the kingdom “for such a time as this” and her decision to go to the king form the turning point of the book.
The king's sleepless night and Haman's humiliation are the book's clearest picture of hidden providence at work.
Esther names her people and her enemy, and Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
The day of destruction becomes a day of deliverance, and the feast of Purim is established.
